title: Deferred Flush and Token Handoff Protocol
content:
Summary:

This note proposes a pragmatic protocol for coordinating deferred output flushes, partial-token handoffs, and cancellation semantics across the serving runtime, kernel scheduler, and KV cache. It is motivated by three practical trade-offs we observe in production: (1) emitting every partial token immediately increases service jitter and networking overhead, (2) aggressive batching/flush consolidation improves throughput but risks wasted work on canceled in-flight generations, and (3) kernel-level quantization and memory layout make preemption expensive unless coordinated with higher-level emission boundaries.

Goals:
- Reduce small-payload churn on client-facing streams while preserving low p95 latency for short responses.
- Bound wasted GPU cycles for canceled requests by introducing lightweight emission checkpoints that are cheap to roll back.
- Make cancellation observable and deterministic across multi-stage serving (router -> worker -> kernel).
- Ensure KV cache remains consistent with emitted prefixes and can be used for warm-started resumptions.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Serving runtime uses continuous batching with opportunistic kernel launches; kernels are optimized for multi-token sequences and have nontrivial setup cost.
- KV cache is append-only per request until a flush boundary is committed; cache eviction and checkpointing are supported via sequence-number watermarks.
- Network streaming is HTTP/2 or WebSocket frames carrying framed token deltas; clients may disconnect abruptly.

Key ideas (high-level):
1) Emission Checkpoints (EC): introduce a lightweight, monotonic sequence number per request (ec.seq) that marks safe-to-emit boundaries. The runtime only advertises tokens to the network when their associated ec.seq is committed. Inside the worker, partial token output is still generated and used for next-token conditioning, but is not sent to the client until EC commit.

2) Deferred Flush with Hysteresis: instead of emitting every partial token, the runtime groups token writes into flush windows controlled by a two-parameter hysteresis: max_flush_latency (ms) and max_flush_tokens. A flush triggers when either threshold is hit or when the EC is marked critical (see below). Hysteresis reduces tiny frames and provides predictable batching for kernel scheduling.

3) Cancellation Window and Safe-Rollback Points: cancellations are treated as time-bound signals. If a cancellation arrives before the last committed EC, we can safely discard uncommitted partial work with no client-visible effect. If cancellation arrives post-commit, we must send a termination marker but keep emitted prefix durable in the KV cache and logs. The runtime exposes two windows: safe_rollback_before_ec (default N ECs) and forced_termination_after (time limit).

4) Kernel-aware EC Boundaries: kernels expose a light API to indicate cheap rollback points in the instruction stream (e.g., kv_sync points). The scheduler prefers to align EC commit boundaries with kernel rollback points when possible, reducing the cost of preemption. If alignment cannot be achieved within max_flush_latency, the runtime will still commit an EC but annotate it as non-rollbackable (higher-cost).

Detailed protocol flow:
- Request start: router assigns request to worker shard. worker initializes ec.seq = 0, creates an in-memory pending buffer (per-request) and a transient KV delta buffer.
- Token generation loop (worker): each time the generator produces a partial token delta (could be byte-level or token-level depending on tokenizer), it appends the delta to the pending buffer and to the KV delta buffer. It also records the kernel position marker and a suggested ec_hint (cheap|moderate|expensive) returned by kernel runtime.
- Flush decision: a local flush controller evaluates hysteresis: if pending buffer length >= max_flush_tokens OR oldest pending delta age >= max_flush_latency OR ec_hint == cheap OR external critical flag (e.g., end-of-stream) -> commit EC.
- EC commit: increment ec.seq, atomically swap pending buffer into committed buffer, persist KV delta buffer to a short-lived durable layer (in-RAM with WAL) and mark as committed_ec:<seq>. Emit framed stream messages to client including the ec.seq in metadata. Start a short confirm-timer (ack expected by router) to guard against lost frames.
- Cancellation: on cancel request, router forwards cancel to worker with the last-observed client ack for ec.seq. Worker inspects: if cancel arrives with client_ack < committed_ec -> the cancel is before the last committed boundary; worker truncates pending buffer (safe rollback) and abandons any queued kernel prefetch. If cancel arrives with client_ack >= committed_ec -> worker sends termination marker frame and keeps committed buffers durable. In all cases worker signals scheduler to deprioritize the request; if request is currently executing an expensive kernel region with no rollback point, mark kernel as teardown-candidate and allow it to finish to simplify correctness (we trade some wasted cycles for simpler kernel rollback semantics).

Resumption and KV cache semantics:
- Committed ECs are the only points from which a resumed generation may continue. The KV cache stores per-ec watermarks (kv.watermark = ec.seq) and the full prefix needed to rehydrate the model state. Resumption flow reads last committed watermark, loads KV deltas up to that watermark, and restarts generator with the correct conditioning.

- For partial, uncommitted tokens we do NOT persist to long-term KV store. If the request must be resumed after a disconnect that occurred before EC commit, the client will need to replay the prompt or request a client-side re-send. This keeps the KV store clean and bounds persistence overhead.

Metrics and observability primitives:
- emit_ec_rate: ECs/sec per worker. Helps tune hysteresis knobs.
- avg_pending_tokens_at_commit: measure of batching effectiveness.
- rollback_rate: fraction of ECs discarded due to cancellation. Target extremely low (<=1%) for large workloads.
- expensive_commit_fraction: fraction of commits marked non-rollbackable; we monitor this to signal scheduler-kernel alignment problems.
- client_ack_lag: median and p95 time between emit and client ack; informs confirm-timer sizing.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Lost stream frames: confirm-timer triggers local re-emit for ec.seq if ack not received; confirmed ECs are idempotent based on seq numbers.
- Kernel crashes during non-rollbackable region: system must fallback to conservative behavior: mark EC as poisoned, record state to logs, and surface error to client with suggestion to retry from last committed EC.
- Long-running expensive kernels causing wasted work on cancels: introduce politeness windows where scheduler may preempt lower-priority long-running kernels earlier if cancel rates spike.

Backward compatibility / incremental rollout plan:
- Phase 1: implement EC bookkeeping and deferred flush (no kernel API change). Default hysteresis conservative (low latency).
- Phase 2: add confirm-timer and client_ack metadata to stream frames. Collect metrics and telemetry.
- Phase 3: expose kernel rollback hint API to schedulers and enable kernel-aligned EC commits on selected worker pools.
- Phase 4: enable forced alignment and non-rollbackable commit tracking, plus UI panels in Console for emit_ec_rate and rollback_rate.

Open questions / trade-offs to deliberate:
- Default sizes for max_flush_tokens and max_flush_latency — how to autotune per model and per request shape? (tie to Optimize suggestions?)
- How aggressively to attempt kernel alignment vs. simply absorbing cost of wasted cycles?
- Should we offer a client-side flag to request low-churn mode (favor larger ECs) vs. low-latency mode (emit every token)?
- How to represent partial-token semantics in streaming APIs (byte vs token vs subtoken) so EC semantics are unambiguous to clients?

Appendix: suggested knobs and initial defaults (experimental):
- max_flush_latency: 30 ms
- max_flush_tokens: 2 tokens
- safe_rollback_before_ec: 1 (i.e., uncommitted only)
- confirm_timer: 200 ms (resend if ack missing)

Action items:
- Engineering: prototype EC bookkeeping + deferred flush in worker mainline (owner: Priya)
- Scheduler: add metric hook for expensive_commit_fraction and allow soft-preempt hints (owner: Liam)
- Kernel: define minimal rollback hint API v0 (owner: Sofia)

Notes: This design intentionally prefers explicit commit semantics tied to client-visible emit boundaries. That makes cancellation semantics easier to reason about and simplifies KV cache durability guarantees. It also provides natural hooks for Optimize to recommend per-model hysteresis parameters based on observed token length distributions.

End of draft.
